7.4 4. Latency Analysis: TTFT versus Autoregressive Generation
In local applications such as code autocomplete and interactive conversational search, latency consists of two distinct phases: Time to First Token (TTFT) and Inter-Token Latency (ITL).
Our measurements indicate that prompt evaluation throughput scales inversely with parameter volume. Hermes 3 ingested prompts at 75.57 tokens per second, allowing an initial token response within 350 milliseconds for typical coding queries. In contrast, Phi-4 achieved 30.70 tokens per second, resulting in a noticeable latency delay before output streaming commenced.
For background batch processing (such as automated nightly security scanning or git commit review), overall token throughput governs pipeline completion time. An 8B model processing a 5,000-token codebase audit completes execution in approximately 20 minutes, whereas a 14B model requires over 42 minutes for the identical task.

title: 7  Volume III: Hardware Telemetry and Energy Profiling
text:
7.5 5. Memory Scaling and Context-Window Saturation
A central constraint for local workstations is key-value (KV) cache memory expansion. While consumer GPUs provide 8 GB of high-speed VRAM, loading an 8B model in 4-bit quantization occupies approximately 4.9 GB, leaving 3.1 GB for context buffers and operating system overhead.
When document context exceeds 4,000 tokens, the KV cache expands significantly. If context demands exceed physical VRAM, the runtime must offload tensor operations to host system RAM over the PCIe bus. Our measurements show that PCIe memory offloading causes generation throughput to drop by up to 80%, transforming interactive responses into sluggish batch processing.
Practitioners must calibrate context window limits to ensure that model weights and dynamic KV cache remain entirely within dedicated GPU memory.

7.6 6. Workstation vs. Cloud API Unit Economics
To assess the commercial feasibility of local deployments, we compared workstation electricity and hardware amortisation against commercial cloud API pricing (such as Claude Haiku, GPT-4o-mini, or Gemini Flash).
Assuming an active workload of 100,000 queries per month (averaging 500 input tokens and 200 output tokens per query): - Cloud API Costs: At an average blended rate of $0.40 per million tokens, 70 million tokens per month costs approximately $28.00 per seat, or $336.00 annually per developer. - Local Workstation Costs: Drawing an average of 45 Watts total system power during active inference, 100,000 queries consume approximately 32 kWh of electricity monthly. At European residential rates of €0.30 per kWh, local electrical operating costs equal €9.60 per month. - Financial Crossover: For continuous developer workflows, local execution achieves full financial breakeven against API expenditures within months, while providing complete data privacy and offline operational autonomy.

7.7 7. Hardware Deployment Guidelines
For engineering organizations deploying local LLM workstations, our data supports three core rules:

8B Architectures are the Workstation Sweet Spot: Models with 8 billion parameters (Llama 3.1 8B, Hermes 3) provide the optimal balance of throughput (4–5 tok/s), memory headroom (4.9 GB VRAM), and electrical efficiency (1.69–1.75 tok/J).
Reserve 14B+ Architectures for High-VRAM Workstations: Models exceeding 9 GB should be reserved for workstations equipped with 16 GB VRAM or dedicated server nodes to prevent severe PCIe bus throttling.
Monitor Cold Loading Timeouts: Runtime engines on CPU fallbacks require minimum client timeouts of 300 seconds to prevent artificial request cancellation during initial model loading into RAM.

8.3 Deployment Decision Flowchart
When selecting an architecture for a new workload, follow this decision sequence:

Does the pipeline process untrusted external documents or user inputs?

If yes: deploy llama3.1:8b. Its adversarial rejection prevents indirect system prompt overrides.

Does the pipeline execute long-chain mathematical or deductive reasoning offline?

If yes: deploy phi4:latest. Its 24/25 score provides the highest analytical precision.

Does the pipeline generate runnable executable code?

If yes: mandate automated test sandboxing. Both phi4 and llama3.1 achieved 100% pass rates, but runtime assertions remain mandatory to prevent regressions.

Is interactive latency the primary design constraint?

If yes: avoid 14B models on CPU hardware. Time-to-first-token on 14B models exceeds 120 seconds under CPU execution, whereas 8B models respond in under 17 seconds.

title: 10  Research Dissemination and Analysis Briefs
text:
10.1.1 1. Beyond Prompt Injections: Multi-Dimensional Evaluation
Most AI security evaluations stop at surface-level prompt injection. Evaluators present models with basic instruction overrides, count refusals, and declare systems secure.
In our empirical evaluations, prompt injection resistance represents less than 20% of operational failure modes. In real-world enterprise deployments, models fail through broken JSON structures, silent logic regressions in generated functions, and semantic fragility under superficial prompt phrasing.
Our expanded harness evaluates five concrete operational dimensions: 1. Execution-Grounded Verification: Testing generated code against hidden unit tests in isolated subprocesses. hermes3:latest scored 0.947 pass@1, failing a subtle string parsing edge case that qualitative LLM judges scored 5/5. Both phi4:latest and llama3.1:8b achieved 1.000 pass@1. 2. Semantic Perturbation Invariance: Evaluating stability across isomorphic prompt pairs where surface entities are swapped while mathematical topologies remain identical. 3. Schema Determinism: Measuring syntax integrity and key fidelity across temperature variations (\(T = 0.0\) to \(1.0\)). 4. Epistemic Authority Resistance: Testing whether candidate models refute fabricated premises asserted under simulated authority titles. 5. Hardware Power Telemetry: Continuous 100 millisecond power polling measuring Joules per query and tokens per Joule.



10.1.2 2. The Efficiency Frontier: Parameter Scale vs. Operational Fitness
A prevalent industry assumption asserts that parameter count directly predicts operational competence. Our data contradicts this assumption:

llama3.1:8b (4.9 GB on disk) matched the cognitive output of 14B architectures across three of five categories, scoring 22/25 points.
In adversarial evaluations, llama3.1:8b scored 4.6/5.0, rejecting all five core injection vectors while operating at half the memory consumption of larger models.
On mobile GPU silicon, llama3.1:8b generated 4.10 tokens per second while consuming 145.66 Joules per query (1.69 tokens per Joule).
Larger 14B models incurred significant latency penalties under CPU memory paging, taking over 120 seconds per query on complex logic prompts.




10.1.3 3. Self-Hosted Workstations vs. Frontier Cloud APIs
When deciding between local deployments and commercial cloud endpoints, engineering teams must evaluate three structural trade-offs:

Data Sovereignty: Local Ollama execution guarantees that proprietary source code, patient data, and internal schemas never leave the local network.
Predictable Unit Economics: At 100,000 monthly queries, cloud API expenditures reach approximately $336.00 annually per developer seat. A local workstation drawing 45 Watts consumes roughly €9.60 per month in electrical power, achieving financial breakeven within months.
Latency and Batch Execution: Cloud endpoints provide high throughput for burst traffic, whereas local execution excels at private background linting, offline analysis, and air-gapped automation.




10.1.4 4. Advanced Adversarial Red-Teaming Matrix
Our security test suite extends beyond basic jailbreaks to evaluate eight sophisticated attack surfaces: - Multi-turn crescendo conversational escalation - Base64 and rot13 encoding evasion - Steganographic injection using zero-width unicode characters - Cipher translation laundering through low-resource languages - Algorithmic resource-exhaustion denial-of-service loops - System prompt extraction via roleplay deception - Verbatim memorization and training data exfiltration - Many-shot in-context priming attacks
